title: UNIT 3: BIOCHEMICAL MOLECULES
notes:
✓ Biochemical molecules are substances found in living organisms that are important for cell structure and life processes.

→ They are grouped into two major categories: inorganic and organic molecules.

◆ Inorganic molecules → mainly water and inorganic ions.
◆ Organic molecules → carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

→ Organic molecules generally contain carbon and hydrogen and are built through covalent bonding.

title: 3.1.1 INORGANIC MOLECULES: WATER
notes:
✓ Water (H₂O) is an inorganic molecule made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. It forms about 70–95% of cell mass and is essential for life.

→ Water is a polar molecule because oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen. This gives oxygen a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another.

title: 3.1.1.1 PROPERTIES OF WATER
notes:
◆ Solvent → dissolves ions and polar molecules, allowing substances to move and react in cells.
◆ High specific heat capacity → resists sudden temperature changes and helps organisms maintain stable temperatures.
◆ High latent heat of vaporization → requires much energy to evaporate, making evaporation useful for cooling, such as sweating.
◆ Density/freezing property → ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats and insulates water below it, helping aquatic life survive.
◆ Cohesion → water molecules attract each other.
◆ Adhesion → water molecules attract other surfaces; together with cohesion, this helps water move through plant vessels.
◆ Surface tension → strong attraction between water molecules at the surface allows some small organisms to live or move on the water surface.
◆ High boiling and freezing points → hydrogen bonding gives water relatively high boiling and freezing points, important for stable aquatic environments.

title: 3.1.2 INORGANIC IONS
notes:
✓ Inorganic ions are charged particles formed when atoms gain or lose electrons. They may be positively charged (cations) or negatively charged (anions). They occur freely dissolved in body fluids/cytoplasm or associated with organic substances.

→ In the human body they are commonly called minerals and are important for maintaining normal cellular functions and homeostasis.

title: CLASSIFICATION OF INORGANIC IONS
notes:
✓ Based on dietary requirements, minerals are classified as:

→ Macronutrients → required in relatively larger amounts.
◆ Examples: sodium, phosphorus, magnesium, potassium, sulfur and chloride.

→ Micronutrients → required in smaller amounts.
◆ Examples: iron, copper, iodine and manganese.

title: IMPORTANT INORGANIC IONS & THEIR ROLES
notes:
◆ Hydrogen (H⁺) → important for acid–base balance; its concentration is expressed using pH.

◆ Sodium (Na⁺) → major extracellular cation; helps maintain fluid balance, osmotic pressure and normal body functions.

◆ Potassium (K⁺) → major intracellular cation; important for normal cell, nerve and muscle function.

◆ Calcium (Ca²⁺) → important for bones and teeth and also performs important functions in cells and extracellular fluids.

◆ Phosphate (PO₄³⁻) → important in bones and teeth and occurs abundantly inside cells.

◆ Chloride (Cl⁻) → helps maintain osmotic and acid–base balance; needed to form hydrochloric acid in gastric juice and activates salivary amylase.

◆ Iron (Fe) → important in haemoglobin and myoglobin for oxygen transport; also involved in electron transport and enzymes.

◆ Copper (Cu) → required for important proteins and enzymes and contributes to haemoglobin, collagen, elastin and nervous-system development.

◆ Iodine (I) → required for thyroid hormone production, which regulates metabolism and other body functions.

title: MINERAL DEFICIENCY & EXCESS
notes:
✓ Imbalances in mineral concentrations can cause health problems.

◆ Iron deficiency → iron-deficiency anaemia.
◆ Excess iron → hemosiderosis or hemochromatosis.
◆ Abnormal copper metabolism → Wilson disease, causing copper accumulation and organ damage.
◆ Iodine deficiency → reduced thyroid hormone production and may lead to hypothyroidism and goiter.

→ A balanced diet is important for maintaining appropriate mineral levels.

title: 3.1.3 ORGANIC MOLECULES
notes:
✓ Organic molecules are carbon-containing compounds found in living organisms. Carbon can form large and complex molecules through covalent bonding.

→ The four principal groups are:
◆ Carbohydrates
◆ Lipids
◆ Proteins
◆ Nucleic acids

✓ These molecules are essential for cell structure, energy storage, metabolism, growth, repair and genetic information.

title: MONOMERS & POLYMERS
notes:
✓ Many organic molecules are built from smaller units called monomers. Monomers can join through covalent bonds to form polymers.

◆ Carbohydrates → monosaccharides
◆ Lipids → glycerol + fatty acids
◆ Proteins → amino acids
◆ Nucleic acids → nucleotides

title: CARBOHYDRATES
notes:
✓ Carbohydrates are organic macromolecules made mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. They are important sources of energy and also have storage and structural functions.

→ Three main groups:
◆ Monosaccharides
◆ Disaccharides
◆ Polysaccharides

title: MONOSACCHARIDES
notes:
✓ Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and contain one sugar unit. Common examples are glucose, galactose and fructose.

→ They can be classified according to the number of carbon atoms:
◆ Triose → 3 carbons
◆ Pentose → 5 carbons
◆ Hexose → 6 carbons

→ Glucose is especially important in energy metabolism.

title: FUNCTIONS OF MONOSACCHARIDES
notes:
◆ Provide energy during cellular respiration.
◆ Glucose helps produce ATP.
◆ Act as building blocks for larger molecules.
◆ Glucose forms starch, glycogen and cellulose.
◆ Ribose is a component of RNA and ATP.
◆ Deoxyribose is a component of DNA.

title: DISACCHARIDES
notes:
✓ Disaccharides are formed when two monosaccharides join.

◆ Maltose = glucose + glucose
◆ Lactose = glucose + galactose
◆ Sucrose = glucose + fructose

→ Maltose is produced during starch breakdown. Lactose is found in milk. Sucrose is the common transport sugar in plants and table sugar.

title: POLYSACCHARIDES
notes:
✓ Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides, mainly glucose. Important examples are:

◆ Starch → storage carbohydrate in plants; found in roots and seeds.
◆ Glycogen → storage carbohydrate in animals; mainly stored in liver and muscles.
◆ Cellulose → structural carbohydrate forming much of the plant cell wall.

✓ Starch and glycogen provide stored energy, while cellulose provides strength and support.

title: CARBOHYDRATE FOOD TESTS
notes:
◆ Benedict's test → identifies reducing sugars. A blue Benedict's solution can change toward green/yellow/orange and finally brick-red depending on the amount of reducing sugar after heating.

◆ Iodine test → identifies polysaccharides. Starch gives a blue-black colour.

title: LIPIDS
notes:
✓ Lipids are diverse organic molecules that are insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents such as ether, chloroform and acetone. They contain mainly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

◆ Examples include fats, oils and cholesterol.

→ Fats → generally solid at room temperature.
→ Oils → generally liquid at room temperature.

✓ Lipids are associated with fatty acids and glycerol.

title: FATTY ACIDS
notes:
✓ Fatty acids contain a carboxyl (-COOH) group and a hydrocarbon chain.

→ Unsaturated fatty acids → contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds. They are commonly found in oils.
◆ Monounsaturated → one double bond.
◆ Polyunsaturated → more than one double bond.
→ Saturated fatty acids → contain no carbon-carbon double bonds and are commonly associated with solid animal fats.

title: PHOSPHOLIPIDS
notes:
✓ Phospholipids are lipids containing a phosphate group. They have:

◆ Hydrophilic head → attracted to water.
◆ Hydrophobic tails → repel water.

→ Because of this arrangement, phospholipids form the bilayer of cell membranes, with hydrophilic heads facing watery environments and hydrophobic tails facing inward.

title: MAJOR FUNCTIONS OF LIPIDS
notes:
◆ Long-term energy storage.
◆ Major dietary energy source in fats and oils.
◆ Thermal insulation, especially in animals.
◆ Structural components of cell membranes.
◆ Cholesterol is used as a precursor for vitamin D, bile acids and steroid hormones.
◆ Waxes provide protective and water-resistant coatings on plants and animals.

title: PROTEINS
notes:
✓ Proteins are organic macromolecules made mainly of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen; some also contain sulfur or phosphorus. They are polymers of amino acids and are among the most abundant and functionally diverse molecules in cells.

→ Protein-rich foods include meat, milk, cheese, fish, beans and other foods.

title: AMINO ACIDS
notes:
✓ Amino acids are the monomers of proteins. A typical amino acid has a central carbon bonded to:

◆ Amino group (-NH₂)
◆ Carboxyl group (-COOH)
◆ Hydrogen atom
◆ R group/side chain

→ The R group differs among amino acids. The textbook notes that 20 different amino acids occur in proteins of living organisms.

title: PEPTIDE BONDS & POLYPEPTIDES
notes:
✓ Amino acids join through peptide bonds during a condensation reaction. A molecule of water is removed when the bond forms.

◆ 2 amino acids → dipeptide
◆ Many amino acids → polypeptide
◆ One or more polypeptide chains → protein

→ During digestion, peptide bonds are broken by hydrolysis, producing amino acids that can be absorbed.

title: GLOBULAR & FIBROUS PROTEINS
notes:
→ Globular proteins → fold into compact shapes, are often soluble in water and commonly perform functional roles.
◆ Examples include enzymes, haemoglobin and antibodies.

→ Fibrous proteins → form long strands, are generally insoluble and mainly have structural roles.
◆ Examples include keratin in hair, nails and skin, and collagen in skin, tendons, cartilage, bones and blood-vessel walls.

title: MAJOR FUNCTIONS OF PROTEINS
notes:
1. Structural proteins → provide strength and support; examples include collagen, elastin and keratin.

2. Enzymes → biological catalysts that increase reaction rates by lowering activation energy.

3. Hormones → regulate physiological processes such as growth and reproduction; examples include growth hormone and FSH.

4. Respiratory pigments → transport or provide oxygen; examples include haemoglobin and myoglobin.

5. Transport proteins → move substances across membranes or through body fluids.

6. Motor proteins → involved in muscle movement; examples include actin and myosin.

7. Storage proteins → store amino acids or metal ions; examples include ferritin, ovalbumin and casein.

8. Toxins → some proteins produced by organisms can damage or kill cells.

title: PROTEIN TESTS
notes:
◆ Biuret test → proteins react in an alkaline solution with copper ions and produce a mauve/purple colour.

◆ Xanthoproteic test → identifies proteins containing certain aromatic amino acids such as phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan through a characteristic colour reaction.

title: NUCLEIC ACIDS
notes:
✓ Nucleic acids are biological macromolecules made of nucleotides. They contain a sugar, phosphate group and nitrogen-containing bases. Their major role is storing, transmitting and using genetic information.

→ Two major types:
◆ DNA → deoxyribonucleic acid
◆ RNA → ribonucleic acid

title: NUCLEOTIDES
notes:
✓ Each nucleotide contains three components:

◆ Nitrogenous base
◆ Pentose sugar
◆ Phosphate group

→ DNA bases → Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C).
→ RNA bases → Adenine (A), Uracil (U), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C).

→ DNA contains deoxyribose sugar, while RNA contains ribose sugar.

title: DNA vs RNA
notes:
→ DNA → usually double-stranded, contains deoxyribose and thymine, is very stable and stores genetic information for many proteins.
◆ It carries genes and can replicate during cell division.

→ RNA → usually single-stranded, contains ribose and uracil, is smaller and less stable. It participates in protein synthesis and has several forms.

✓ Easy memory: DNA = long-term genetic information;
RNA = uses/carries genetic information for protein production.

title: TYPES OF RNA
notes:
◆ mRNA (messenger RNA) → carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes.

◆ tRNA (transfer RNA) → brings amino acids needed for protein synthesis.

◆ rRNA (ribosomal RNA) → combines with proteins to form ribosomes.

notes:
◆ Water → polar inorganic molecule + hydrogen bonds
◆ Inorganic ions → minerals needed for body functions
◆ Carbohydrates → energy + storage + structure
◆ Monosaccharide → 1 sugar unit
◆ Disaccharide → 2 sugar units
◆ Polysaccharide → many sugar units
◆ Starch → plant storage
◆ Glycogen → animal storage
◆ Cellulose → plant cell wall
◆ Lipids → energy storage + membranes + insulation
◆ Phospholipid → hydrophilic head + hydrophobic tails
◆ Protein → amino-acid polymer
◆ Peptide bond → links amino acids
◆ Globular → functional proteins
◆ Fibrous → structural proteins
◆ Nucleic acids → DNA + RNA
◆ Nucleotide → sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base
◆ DNA → stores genetic information
◆ RNA → helps express genetic information and make proteins
